questions.q: What does the -ggdb option do in `gcc -ggdb fibber.c -o fibber_bin`?
choices: Optimizes the binary so it runs faster under GDB
Adds GDB debugging symbols to the binary
Automatically launches GDB on the compiled program
questions.explain: -ggdb adds debugging symbols for GDB. The output file is named by -o fibber_bin.

questions.q: Which command compiles echo.c into an executable named echo_bin with GDB debugging symbols?
questions.explain: gcc is the compiler and gdb is the debugger. The source file is the input and -o names the output. Swapping them would treat echo_bin as the input and overwrite echo.c.

questions.q: What shell command checks whether gdb is installed by printing its version?
questions.explain: Likewise, `gcc --version` checks gcc. If either one says 'command not found', install both with `sudo apt-get install -y gcc gdb`.

questions.q: Which gcc flags build debugging symbols into a binary so that GDB's list command can show its source?
questions.explain: -g and -ggdb both enable symbols. -o names the output file, and -q is a gdb option (quiet), not a gcc one.

questions.q: When GDB loads a binary it prints '(No debugging symbols found in ./fibber_bin)'. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The binary was compiled without -g or -ggdb
The program has not been run yet
The path to the binary is wrong
questions.explain: Debugging symbols come from compiling with -g or -ggdb. Symbols are read when the file is loaded, before anything runs. --quiet only hides the startup banner, and a wrong path gives a 'No such file' error.

questions.q: Which GDB output shows that the binary was built with debugging symbols?
questions.explain: With debug info, GDB can map an address to a source file and line number. Without it, GDB reports only addresses and function names.

questions.q: The gdb command-line options --quiet and -q are equivalent.
questions.explain: -q is the short form of --quiet.

questions.q: Which of these load fibber_bin into GDB so it's ready to run?
choices: gdb -q, then at the (gdb) prompt: file ./fibber_bin
gdb -q, then at the (gdb) prompt: run ./fibber_bin
questions.explain: You can give the path on the command line, before or after -q, or load it later with `file <path>`. Anything after run is passed to the program as command-line arguments. It does not choose which executable to load.

questions.q: You started GDB with just `gdb -q`. What one-word command loads an executable at the (gdb) prompt (it's followed by the path)?
questions.explain: For example: `file ./fibber_bin`. GDB then prints 'Reading symbols from ./fibber_bin...'.

questions.q: Which commands exit GDB from the (gdb) prompt?
questions.explain: q is short for quit. c is short for continue, and d is short for delete.

questions.q: You type quit while the program you're debugging is stopped at a breakpoint. What does GDB do?
choices: It exits immediately and leaves the program running in the background
It warns that a debugging session is active and the inferior process will be killed, then asks you to confirm
It refuses to quit until the program has run to completion
It continues the program to completion and then exits
questions.explain: GDB prints 'A debugging session is active. Inferior 1 [process N] will be killed. Quit anyway? (y or n)'.

questions.q: What does the run (r) command do?
choices: It resumes a program that is stopped at a breakpoint
It runs the program and always stops at its entry point
It runs the loaded program as if you had invoked it from the command line, stopping only if it hits a breakpoint
It compiles the source file and runs the result
questions.explain: With no breakpoints, fibber_bin prints its full output and GDB reports that the inferior exited. Resuming is continue, and stopping at the entry point is start.

questions.q: echo_bin is loaded in GDB. What command runs it with hi as argv[1]?
questions.explain: Arguments after run are passed to the program exactly as they would be on the command line. The program then prints 'You entered hi for argv[1]'.

questions.q: How does start differ from run?
choices: start sets a temporary breakpoint on the program's entry point, so execution stops there
start only loads the program and doesn't execute any of it
questions.explain: start works like run, but it stops right away at a temporary breakpoint. In the examples GDB prints 'Temporary breakpoint 1, 0x0000555555555189 in main ()'.

questions.q: Like run, start accepts command-line arguments for the program, for example `start hi`.
questions.explain: `start hi` runs echo_bin with hi as argv[1] and stops at the temporary breakpoint.

questions.q: The program is stopped at the temporary breakpoint that start set. What one-letter command resumes execution?
questions.explain: c is short for continue. GDB prints 'Continuing.', and the program runs until it hits another breakpoint or exits.

questions.q: fibber_bin has a breakpoint on fibbonacci, and you keep typing c. main's loop calls fibbonacci(i) for i = 0, 1, 2, ... The first three hits show n=0, n=1 and n=2. The disassembly shows that fibbonacci computes n-1 and makes that recursive call before the n-2 call. What value of n will the fourth hit show?
questions.explain: fibbonacci(0) and fibbonacci(1) return immediately because n <= 1, so the first three hits are main's loop calls for i = 0, 1 and 2. fibbonacci(2) then calls fibbonacci(1) recursively, and the breakpoint fires on recursive calls too.

questions.q: With no breakpoints set, you run fibber_bin under GDB and the output ends with '[Inferior 1 (process 60848) exited normally]'. What does that mean?
choices: The program ran to completion and exited
The program is paused at its last instruction
The program could not be loaded
questions.explain: The 'inferior' is the program being debugged. With nothing to stop it, it ran all the way through.

questions.q: What is the short form of the break command?
questions.explain: `break main` and `b main` do the same thing.

questions.q: What command sets a breakpoint at the start of the function fibbonacci?
questions.explain: A breakpoint can be set by symbol name. GDB replies with something like 'Breakpoint 2 at 0x1169'.

questions.q: Which commands list the current breakpoints?
questions.explain: info break and info b are shorter forms of info breakpoints. list shows source code, not breakpoints.

questions.q: disas shows an instruction at 0x000055555555520e. What command sets a breakpoint exactly at that address?
questions.explain: The * in front of a number tells GDB it's a memory address, not a symbol name or line number. GDB confirms with 'Breakpoint 3 at 0x55555555520e'.

questions.q: In info b output, the line 'breakpoint already hit 3 times' appears under breakpoint 2. What does it mean?
choices: Breakpoint 2 has been set three times
Execution has stopped at breakpoint 2 three times so far
Breakpoint 2 will be deleted after three more hits
Three breakpoints share the same address
questions.explain: info b keeps a hit count for each breakpoint, for example after you've continued into fibbonacci three times.

questions.q: What is the difference between clear and delete?
choices: clear removes every breakpoint; delete removes one
clear disables a breakpoint; delete removes it
clear takes a location (a symbol name, or * followed by an address); delete takes a breakpoint number from info b
questions.explain: Two examples: `clear fibbonacci` or `clear *0x00000000000011a9` versus `delete 3`. Disabling is done with disable.

questions.q: Which command uses clear to remove the breakpoint at absolute address 0x00000000000011a9?
questions.explain: clear takes a symbol name or * followed by an absolute address. delete takes a breakpoint number, not an address.

questions.q: info b lists your breakpoint on main as number 3. What command deletes it by its number?
questions.explain: d is short for delete. Afterward, info b shows 'No breakpoints or watchpoints.' if it was the only breakpoint.

questions.q: What command removes the breakpoint on fibbonacci by naming the function, without looking up its breakpoint number?
questions.explain: clear accepts a symbol name, so you don't need the number from info b.

questions.q: Before running, `b main` reports 'Breakpoint 1 at 0x11a9'. After r, the same breakpoint is listed at 0x00005555555551a9. Why?
choices: GDB moved the breakpoint to a different function when the program started
Before the program runs, the address is only an offset into the executable; GDB learns the real address once the program is loaded into memory
0x11a9 was a breakpoint number, not an address
The program recompiled itself when it started
questions.explain: The debugger can't know where the program will be loaded until it actually runs. The OS may also randomize the load address (ASLR).

questions.q: Before running, the breakpoints were at main = 0x11a9 and fibbonacci = 0x1169. After r, main's breakpoint shows 0x5555555551a9. What address (in hex) does fibbonacci's breakpoint show now?
questions.explain: The load base is 0x5555555551a9 - 0x11a9 = 0x555555554000, and every offset shifts by that amount: 0x555555554000 + 0x1169 = 0x555555555169.

questions.q: What is Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR)?
choices: GDB randomizing the numbers it assigns to breakpoints
The compiler shuffling the order of functions in the source
The OS randomizing where an executable is loaded in memory, to help mitigate some security vulnerabilities
A GDB feature that picks a random entry point
questions.explain: Because the load location can change, a breakpoint's run-time address isn't known until the program has been started.

questions.q: If you repeat the same steps on your own machine, the run-time breakpoint addresses will always exactly match the ones in the examples.
questions.explain: Where an executable is loaded can differ between systems and between runs, partly because of ASLR. The offsets within the binary stay the same, but the absolute addresses can change.

questions.q: What does `disable 2` do?
choices: Breakpoint 2 stays in the list but no longer stops execution
It disables every breakpoint except number 2
It makes breakpoint 2 stop execution twice
questions.explain: info b still lists the breakpoint, with n in the Enb column. `enable 2` turns it back on.

questions.q: Breakpoint 1 is disabled. What command turns it back on?
questions.explain: Afterward, info b shows y in the Enb column for breakpoint 1.

questions.q: Which column of the info b output tells you whether a breakpoint is currently active?
questions.explain: Enb means enabled: y or n. Num is the number used by delete, disable and enable. Address and What show where the breakpoint is.

questions.q: A disabled breakpoint disappears from the info b output.
questions.explain: It stays listed, with n in the Enb column. Only delete or clear removes it.

questions.q: Breakpoint 1 is on main and breakpoint 2 is on fibbonacci. You've already stopped in fibbonacci three times. You type `disable 2` and then c. What happens?
choices: It stops at the next call to fibbonacci
The program prints the rest of its output and exits normally without stopping again
questions.explain: Execution is already past main's breakpoint, and fibbonacci's breakpoint is disabled, so nothing stops the program before it exits.

questions.q: Disabled breakpoints are automatically re-enabled when you restart the program with r.
questions.explain: In the example, after re-running, info b still showed breakpoint 2 with Enb n until `enable 2` was entered.

questions.q: Why would you disable a breakpoint instead of deleting it?
choices: delete only works on temporary breakpoints
Disabled breakpoints still stop the program but print less output
To keep it from firing for now while keeping it around so you can turn it back on later with enable
questions.explain: One example: switch off a breakpoint in a heavily called function like fibbonacci, let the program run, then re-enable it without having to set it again.

questions.q: When the program is stopped, what does list (with no arguments) show?
choices: Source code around the current location
The assembly of the current function
questions.explain: For example, stopped at line 13 of fibber.c, list shows the lines around line 13.

questions.q: What command shows the source code before and after the function fibbonacci?
questions.explain: The form is `list <function name>`.

questions.q: What command shows the source code around line 13 of fibber.c?
questions.explain: The form is `list <source file name>:<line number>`.

questions.q: In which situation is the list command of no use?
choices: Debugging fibber_bin that you compiled from fibber.c with -ggdb
Debugging echo_bin that you compiled from echo.c with -g
Reverse engineering an opaque binary you have no source code for
Debugging a program you built from source with symbols enabled
questions.explain: list needs both the source code and a binary built with symbols (-g or -ggdb). An opaque binary has neither.

questions.q: Right after a list command, you press Enter at an empty (gdb) prompt. What happens?
choices: GDB lists the next lines of source
GDB shows the same lines again
questions.explain: Pressing Enter repeats list, which continues from where the last listing ended. At the end of the file, GDB says something like 'Line number 23 out of range; ./fibber.c has 22 lines.'

questions.q: What is the short form of the disassemble command?
questions.explain: For example, `disas main` or `disas` on its own.

questions.q: What does disas show when you give it no arguments?
choices: Assembly of main, no matter where you're stopped
Assembly around the current location, i.e. the function you're stopped in
Only the raw bytes of the current instruction
questions.explain: To disassemble something else, give it an address or symbol name, for example `disas main`.

questions.q: Which option to disassemble also shows the raw bytes that make up each instruction?
questions.explain: /r stands for raw bytes. For example, `disas /r fibbonacci` shows lines like '79 71   addi sp,sp,-48'.

questions.q: Which option to disassemble mixes source code lines with the assembly?
questions.explain: /m stands for mix. Each source line is printed above the instructions generated for it. This requires a binary built with symbols.

questions.q: How do you get both raw bytes and mixed source code in a single disassembly of fibbonacci?
questions.explain: The two options must be combined as /rm, written right after disassemble. /r alone gives only the bytes, and /m alone gives only the source mix.

questions.q: What does the => marker in disas output indicate?
choices: The instruction at the current location, i.e. the next one to execute
An instruction that has a breakpoint on it
The first instruction of the function
questions.explain: For example, after stopping at a breakpoint at main+101, disas puts => next to <+101>.

questions.q: main starts at 0x5555555551a9. After `b *0x000055555555520e`, info b shows that breakpoint's location as <main+101>. What does +101 mean?
choices: The instruction is 101 bytes past the start of main
The breakpoint has been hit 101 times
questions.explain: 0x5555555551a9 + 101 (0x65) = 0x55555555520e. Instructions vary in size, so a byte offset is not the same as an instruction count.

questions.q: What does `x/10i fibbonacci` do?
choices: It prints 10 instructions starting at the address of fibbonacci, once
It prints fibbonacci's instructions every time the program stops
questions.explain: x examines memory, and the i format shows that memory as instructions. 10 is the count. It accepts any address or symbol.

questions.q: How does `display/10i $rip` differ from `x/10i $rip`?
choices: display reprints the 10 instructions every time the program stops; x prints them once
display shows source code while x shows assembly
x updates automatically while display prints once
questions.explain: After display/10i $rip, each stop prints '1: x/10i $rip' followed by the next 10 instructions, so you always see what's about to execute.

questions.q: On 64-bit x86, which command prints the next 10 instructions to execute every time the program stops?
questions.explain: In 64-bit x86 code the instruction pointer is RIP, written $rip in GDB. $eip is the 32-bit name. x prints only once. Without the $, GDB treats rip as a symbol name instead of a register.

questions.q: On RISC-V or ARM, what register expression completes `display/10i ___` so that it follows the next instruction to execute?
questions.explain: On ARM and RISC-V this register is called the program counter, so the command is `display/10i $pc`.

questions.q: In 32-bit x86 code, what is the instruction pointer register called?
questions.explain: EIP is the 32-bit name and RIP is the 64-bit name. PC (program counter) is the name used on ARM and RISC-V. SP is the stack pointer.
